prompt:
Reddit post, r/houseplants.
Title: Pruning tips? Organic basil plant I purchased May 2019

An automatic image classifier was also run on each photo. It only knows 5 classes:
- healthy: no visible problem
- watering: wilting or withering from too little or too much water
- fungal_bacterial: leaf spots, rust, anthracnose, blight, rot, bacterial wilt
- pest: visible insects or mites (trained almost only on cochineal scale on cactus)
- other: anything else, e.g. sunburn, nutrient or mineral problems, viruses, leaf tip necrosis, cold damage

The classifier is not perfect. It was trained mostly on curated dataset photos, not on phone photos like these,
and on such photos it is often wrong while still reporting a very high probability. Treat it as one weak hint:
rely on what you see in the photos and on the post first.

Classifier output (probability of each class):
Photo 1: healthy 60%, watering 39%, fungal_bacterial 1%, other 0%, pest 0%

What is wrong with my plant?
answer:
The plant looks basically healthy. Its leaves are green and firm, and I don't see obvious pests, spots, or wilting. The problem is structural: a woody, bare stalk from years of pruning in the wrong places.

**About the woody stalk:** Basil doesn't regrow from bare, woody wood, so cutting into the stalk where there are no leaves or buds usually won't produce new shoots. You have two reasonable options:

- **Cut it back to a node with leaves or a visible bud.** I can see small green buds higher up on the stalk, and the cut tips look green. Trim just above one of those nodes. The stalk may sprout new side shoots there.
- **Remove it entirely** at the soil line or just above the lowest leaf cluster. The leafy part of the plant will be fine, and it will put energy into the healthy growth.

**Going forward, prune correctly:** Cut stems just above a pair of leaves, so two new shoots branch out from that node. Pinch off flower buds as they form, since flowering makes basil woody and bitter. Never strip more than about a third of the plant at once.

**The seedlings:** The two small plants came from seeds the original plant dropped. They're crowding the pot and competing with the main plant. You can keep the larger one and gently remove or transplant the others. Also check the tiny plant at the bottom to confirm it's basil and not a weed.
